statements.t: We are operating our Lost Creek Project, our flagship in situ recovery (“ISR”) mining facility, and our Shirley Basin Project, our second ISR uranium mine.

We utilize ISR to recover uranium at our Lost Creek Property and Shirley Basin Project, which are both located in Wyoming and are the only two mineral properties that we currently deem to be individually material.

Although many of these initiatives remain in proposed or early stages, and their timing, final form, and ultimate effect on the Company cannot be predicted with certainty, they collectively reflect a sustained commitment to nuclear energy and domestic fuel-supply security that the Company believes strengthens the long-term demand outlook for domestic uranium production.
Although we expected the average production grade from wells in MU2 to decrease because the HHs

are now in the latter part of their production curve, for the reasons described below, we were unable to offset that decrease as expected by continuing to add HHs in MU1 Phase 2, increasing flow rates by bringing a sand filtration system online, and other process improvements.

Production grades are expected to vary from quarter to quarter as we move through mine units, and average production grades in Lost Creek mine units, including MU1 and MU2, have generally outperformed our estimates in total.

Average production grades are expected to increase as we move into new mine units that have not previously been subject to ISR operations, including mine unit five (“MU5”), which is our next planned mine unit.

The filtration system has been effective in decreasing fines and increasing production flow rates, but our ability to utilize the system effectively was impacted more than we expected by constraints in our capacity to manage wastewater generated when backflushing the filtration system.
We renewed exploration activities in the Great Divide Basin (“GDB”), Wyoming in the third quarter of 2025, beginning with our Lost Solider Project.

Although the geology of the project is largely understood with the benefit of data from approximately 4,000 historical drill holes, additional hydrogeologic data gathering and characterization are underway to enable us to better plan for potential permitting and development of the site.

During the third quarter of 2026, we completed pump testing of the last of three aquifer-test well clusters that we installed prior to the quarter and continued work on baseline environmental studies in anticipation of possible permitting of the project.
We also significantly advanced work on a technical report for the project during the quarter.

In 2010, we drilled 159 exploration holes (for a total of 101,950 feet) that confirmed numerous individual roll front systems occurring within several stratigraphic horizons correlative to mineralized horizons in the Lost Creek Project.
In the fourth quarter of 2025, we began exploration drilling at our North Hadsell Project, also in the GDB north of Lost Creek.

In another project and industry first, various mine solutions at the Company’s Lost Creek plant were being tested during the third quarter utilizing experimental UVvis technology capable of continuously measuring uranium concentration.
In 2026, we expect to sell a total of 700,000 pounds of U 3 O 8 at an average price per pound sold of approximately $67.00 for revenues of approximately $46.9 million.

Of those 700,000 pounds, 210,000 pounds were contracted in 2024 with a combination of base-escalated and market-based pricing, 75,000 pounds of which we expect to deliver in the fourth quarter of 2026.

We expect to deliver a total of 700,000 pounds of U 3 O 8 in 2026, including the 460,000 pounds that we delivered during the first three quarters and 240,000 pounds that we expect to deliver in the fourth quarter.

Operation of the sand filtration system commenced in July 2026, and while it has been effective in decreasing fines and increasing production flow rates, our ability to utilize the system effectively was impacted more than expected by constraints in our capacity to manage wastewater generated when backflushing the system.

Correspondingly, there will be no depletion allocated to future periods of the Company since those costs were expensed previously, resulting in both lower inventory costs and cost of sales, and results of operations with higher gross profit and lower gross loss than if we would have been in the production stage.

Including the 460,000 pounds that we delivered during the first three quarters and 240,000 pounds that we expect to deliver in the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect to make deliveries under sales contracts of 700,000 pounds of U 3 O 8 in 2026, which is 300,000 pounds less than our previous guidance, at an average price of $67 per pound for total product sales revenue of $46.9 million.

Due to lower than expected production in 2026, we entered into these transactions to increase our ability to satisfy delivery commitments in the fourth quarter of 2026 and in 2027 from our inventory and new production and avoid purchasing pounds of U 3 O 8 at spot prices.
We expect to spend approximately $4.6 million during the fourth quarter of 2026 and approximately $3.8 million in 2027 to finalize the production facility.

We expect to incur additional capital expenditures for Shirley Basin in 2028 or later for additional wastewater treatment equipment to facilitate restoration activities that is not essential for production operations.
We expect to spend approximately $23 million on this project during 2026 and approximately $11 million in 2027 to complete the facility.
During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we spent $7.7 million on capital expenditures related to this project.

We may elect to defer capital expenditures related to this facility, which will be required for future restoration activities and is expected to allow us to increase flow rates and production, but is not essential for production operations at current levels.

Although we may elect to defer capital expenditures as described above, we anticipate the planned capital projects at Shirley Basin and Lost Creek will be funded by cash on hand, expected operating cash flow, and additional funding, if necessary.

Recognizing that production rates are expected to vary from quarter to quarter, we believe the rate of U 3 O 8 pounds drummed at Lost Creek from U 3 O 8 captured at Lost Creek and Shirley Basin will increase over time as we install additional infrastructure, continue optimization of operations, and implement process improvements.

In addition, we expect to receive final regulatory approval for surface discharge of non-hazardous wastewater, which should not only increase flexibility for wastewater management, but will also provide a water source for flora and fauna.

As a longer-term solution to manage wastewater streams, address constraints on our filtration system, and increase flow rates, we expect to complete construction and commence operation of the wastewater treatment facility at Lost Creek in

To address unplanned maintenance at the Lost Creek plant that has hampered production, we plan to implement the short- and long-term maintenance strategy that was completed in the third quarter of 2026.
To increase average grades at Lost Creek, we plan to move into and commence operations in MU5.
We expect to receive regulatory approval in sufficient time to allow us to commence production operations in MU5 in the first quarter of 2027.
We expect pounds of U 3 O 8 captured at Shirley Basin to increase as we improve operating parameters associated with the early ramp up and optimization of ISR operations.

To further the ramp up of production from the wellfield, in the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect to complete the workover, gravel packing, and other improvements to the wells in HH 1-1 and HH 1-2 that are underway.
We also expect to bring online 76 additional production and injection wells in HH 1-3.

We expect to install wastewater treatment equipment at Shirley Basin in 2028 or later to facilitate restoration activities that is not essential for production operations, with the engineering design based substantially on the design of the Lost Creek wastewater treatment facility.
In October 2026, we received a specialty trailer from the manufacturer to transport uranium from Shirley Basin to Lost Creek and expect to receive an additional trailer in the fourth quarter.
We plan to continue our exploration programs to enhance our ability to leverage existing infrastructure and expand our uranium resource base.
For our Lost Soldier Project, we continue to advance work on a new technical report, which we expect to complete by year-end 2026.

For our Lost Creek South Project, we received regulatory approval from the BLM in October 2026 and have commenced drilling operations of our planned 120-hole drill program, which we expect to complete in the first half of 2027.

estimates.name: Outstanding Share Data

statements.t: During the third quarter, the Company completed the third of three planned aquifer tests and continued to advance a technical report expected by year-end 2026, with a construction decision to follow.

At Lost Creek, Ur-Energy’s flagship uranium ISR mining project, the Company drummed 104,586 pounds of U₃O₈ during the third quarter, a decrease of 25.8% compared to the second quarter, and an increase of 11.8% over the third quarter of 2025.
The Company expects to receive approval to commence production operations in MU5 in the first quarter of 2027.

To further the ramp up of production from the wellfield, the Company expects to complete improvements to the wells in the first two header houses in the near term, and bring additional header houses online throughout the fourth quarter of 2026 and 2027.
In 2026, the Company expects to sell a total of 700,000 pounds of U₃O₈ at an average price of approximately $67.00 per pound for product sales revenues of approximately $46.9 million.
The Company is also engaged in exploration and development activities at a selection of projects in the Great Divide Basin uranium district.
